draft.title: Questioning a text
card: Evaluating a text means asking questions about it before you accept its ideas. A text can be well written and still be one-sided or wrong.
Who
Who made the text? Does the author know the topic, and could they gain from your agreeing?
Why
Why was it made: to inform, to persuade or to sell something? The purpose shapes what is included.
Evidence
What evidence does it give, and is it checkable? Also ask what it leaves out, such as other views or facts that do not suit its argument.
draft.remember: Ask who made a text, why, what evidence it gives and what it leaves out.

a.q: A website says its own brand of trail shoes is the best in Australia. It gives no test results. Which question shows the most doubt about the claim?
opts: What evidence is given, and who made the website?
How many words are on the website?
Does the website have a clear title?
Is the website easy to read on a phone?
a.why: The claim is not backed by evidence, and the seller gains if you agree with it. Asking about evidence and the maker tests the claim. Length, a clear title and ease of reading say nothing about whether the claim is true.
a.clue: Which question tests the claim itself?

b.q: A council leaflet says a new skate park will make the town safer. It quotes only residents who support the park. Which question does this most call for?
opts: What views or facts does the leaflet leave out?
Who designed the font used on the leaflet?
Does the leaflet fit on one page?
Was the leaflet printed on recycled paper?
b.why: The leaflet shows only supporters, so other views may be missing. Asking what is left out checks whether it is one-sided. Font, page count and paper do not affect how fair the ideas are.
b.clue: Think about whose voices are missing.

a.best: What evidence is given, and who made the website?

b.best: What views or facts does the leaflet leave out?

problems.detail: The right option is clearly the longest and the only two-part question. It also repeats the card's words ('evidence', 'who made'), so a student could pick it without understanding the idea.

The three distractors (phone readability, word count, a clear title) are plainly about presentation and have nothing to do with the claim. This makes the question too easy to test evaluation for Year 8. Plausible but weaker questions would test the idea better, such as 'Is the website well designed?' or 'Do other websites sell trail shoes?'

The distractors (font designer, recycled paper, page length) are obviously irrelevant. The right option also echoes the card's 'what it leaves out', so the question can be answered without real thought. Plausible distractors would test the idea better, such as asking who wrote the leaflet when the case calls for missing views.

proposal.title: Questioning a text
card: Evaluating a text means asking questions about it before you accept its ideas. A text can be popular or well made and still be one-sided or wrong.
Who
Who made the text? Does the author know the topic, and could they gain from your agreeing?
Why
Why was it made: to inform, to persuade or to sell something? The purpose shapes what is included.
Evidence
What evidence does it give, and can it be checked by someone else? Also ask what it leaves out, such as other views or facts that do not suit its argument.
proposal.remember: Ask who made a text, why, what evidence it gives and what it leaves out.

a.q: A shoe company's website says its own trail shoes are the best in Australia. It gives no test results. Which question best tests whether the claim is true?
opts: Has anyone outside the company tested the shoes?
Is the website well designed and easy to use?
Do many people visit the website each day?
Do other websites also sell trail shoes?
a.why: The company gains if you agree, and it gives no proof. Tests by someone outside the company would be evidence that others can check. A well-designed or popular website can still make a claim that is false.
a.clue: Who could check the claim without gaining from it?

b.q: Ravi reads a council leaflet. It says a new skate park will make the town safer, and it quotes only residents who support the park. Which question points to the main weakness in the leaflet?
opts: What do residents who oppose the park think?
Which council team produced the leaflet?
How many residents does the leaflet quote?
Is the leaflet written in clear, simple words?
b.why: The leaflet gives only one side, so the views of people against the park are missing. Asking how many residents it quotes is tempting, but more quotes from supporters would still leave out the other side. The leaflet already shows it comes from the council.
b.clue: Whose views does the leaflet not show?

b.best: What do residents who oppose the park think?
